clinician.trajectory_summary: A previously healthy 2-year-old Emirati boy with incomplete immunizations (stopped at 4 months) presented with a 1-week prodrome of upper respiratory symptoms (cold, cough, runny nose) and fever (39.5°C), followed by vomiting and loose stools initially attributed to viral gastroenteritis. He was treated at another ED and discharged, but returned with drowsiness and fluctuating consciousness. On presentation to the ED, he was found to be drowsy (GCS 10-11, fluctuating), febrile (38°C), tachycardic (137/min), hypotensive (80/50 mmHg), with capillary refill time of 4 seconds indicating septic shock. Physical examination revealed no neck stiffness or meningeal signs, but showed erythematous mildly enlarged tonsils. Initial blood work demonstrated leukopenia (WBC 2.73), elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 72.91 mg/L, procalcitonin 95.72 ng/mL), and coagulopathy (PT 19.4 sec, aPTT 41.2 sec, INR 1.65). Empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone 200 mg/kg/day and dexamethasone) were administered early. CT head performed after antibiotic administration showed mild diffuse cerebral edema without raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture was delayed until day 2 after correction of the coagulopathy and revealed CSF findings consistent with bacterial meningitis: elevated protein (105 mg/dL), low glucose (35 mg/dL with blood glucose 80 mg/dL, ratio 0.4), markedly elevated WBC (5566 with 89% polymorphonuclear cells), and Gram-negative coccobacilli on Gram stain. MRI on day 2 showed meningeal enhancement consistent with meningitis. CSF and blood cultures confirmed BLNAR Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis susceptible to ceftriaxone, meropenem, and cefotaxime. On day 7, persistent fever prompted a second blood culture that revealed a BLNAR strain resistant to ceftriaxone but sensitive to meropenem. Antibiotics were changed to meropenem (120 mg/kg/day), and the patient responded well with defervescence. Follow-up MRI prior to discharge (day 16) confirmed resolution of small pockets of pus.
